title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Oil & Gas
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Coast Guard and FBI cyber teams boarded two US-bound energy tankers whose networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors — no operational disruption, and no attribution
items.content_text: A joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement, reported on 16 September, confirmed that cyber teams boarded two foreign-flagged, US-bound energy tankers in the Gulf of Mexico on 21 August and 24 August. The stated purpose was to ensure the integrity of the vessels’ operational and information technology systems “following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised”; the Coast Guard told The Record the networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors, and Rear Adm. Amy Grable, commander of Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that investigators found malicious cyber activity aboard, with a team on one vessel for about four days. The boarding parties combined Coast Guard law enforcement, a vessel inspector and Cyber Protection Team members with FBI Cyber Action Team operators. The first ship is VL Prosperity, a 333-metre Liberian-flagged crude supertanker that loaded at Sidi Kerir, Egypt and was bound for Galveston, Texas; its technical and safety manager is HMM Ocean Service of South Korea — the manager, not a second vessel. The second ship, boarded on 24 August, is described by gCaptain as an unnamed LNG carrier and has not been named by the agencies. Officially there were “no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts”, and HMM Ocean Service says VL Prosperity has been cleared for normal operations. A reported loss of communications for about 30 hours near the Strait of Gibraltar in early August, and claims that attackers reached propulsion, navigation, cargo and fuel or lube-oil systems, originate with Iran’s Mehr News Agency and are unverified. No US agency has attributed the compromise, and no group has claimed it; investigators are examining whether Iran or another actor exploiting the US–Iran conflict was responsible, and whether the two incidents are connected. For oil and gas operators the point is the interface rather than the ship: crude and LNG cargoes bound for US Gulf Coast terminals, and a federal cyber response that reached the berth.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement, quoted by CyberScoop and The Record, with vessel and manager detail from CBS News and gCaptain; propulsion and navigation manipulation claims trace to Iranian state media and are unverified
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; publicly confirmed 16 Sep 2026

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — gas and electric delivery not affected
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and natural gas utility, said in an SEC filing that an unauthorised third party obtained personal information on “a portion of the Company’s customers through one of the Company’s external-facing systems.” BleepingComputer reports the system was a public API with no rate limiting, web application firewall or automated access controls. Exposed data includes names, phone numbers, service and billing addresses, account numbers, billing amounts and partial Social Security numbers. An actor using the alias “4d722e4d656f77” claims to have taken 7.49 million records and has leaked data; CenterPoint has not given a count, and class-action filings allege the intrusion ran from 17 August to 1 September. The company says electric and natural gas services were not affected, and it has notified law enforcement and regulators. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it is scored that way. It belongs on an oil and gas page because gas distribution utilities run exactly this kind of customer-facing API alongside SCADA for pressure and flow — and the useful question is how much those two estates share.
tags: Incident — Customer data theft at a gas and electric utility; no OT impact

items.title: The US puts up to $10 million on the IRGC cyber commander said to direct CyberAv3ngers — energy is on the named target list
items.content_text: On 4 September the US State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on Amir Yaryab, described as a senior official of Iran’s IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) who leads its Cyber Operations Command. The State Department says he directs IRGC-CEC components and affiliated groups including CyberAv3ngers, Dadeh Afzar Arman and Mehrsam Andisheh Saz Nik, and that these groups have targeted critical infrastructure in the United States, Europe and the Middle East, energy and telecommunications among them. Analysis published by Security Boulevard on 9 September also names the Shahid Hemmat and Shahid Shushtari components, and ties Iran-linked groups to attacks on municipal water systems in at least 12 US states this year. The technical background is the joint CISA and FBI warning updated on 22–23 July, which said Iran-affiliated actors attacking PLCs in water and energy had widened their target set beyond Rockwell/Allen-Bradley to Schneider Modicon M340/BMX P34 and Siemens S7-1200 controllers. Those are the controller families found in wellsite automation, compressor stations, tank farms and terminal loading systems. The reward is a policy step, not a new intrusion, and the attributions are US government assessments.
tags: Threat Intelligence — Nation-state actor behind PLC attacks, US reward offer

items.title: Red Heron broke into self-hosted Gitea and walked out with SCADA and HMI source code from an industrial automation vendor
items.content_text: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit published findings on 13 September, reported on 14–15 September, on a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to Red Heron, a Chinese-speaking, PRC-linked actor, exploiting CVE-2026-60004, the CVSS 9.8 Gitea remote code execution flaw fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July. Acronis and Industrial Cyber count at least 11 compromised organisations across Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the United States and Sri Lanka (The Hacker News reports 13 in six countries), including a Canadian renewable energy company, a Taiwanese industrial automation firm, municipal platforms and defence, aerospace and telecoms organisations. From the automation firm the attackers took the source code of a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments, along with IoT integrations and a network sniffer; “hundreds of repositories” were exfiltrated from a single target. The tooling includes the JITTERLY implant, a previously undocumented Linux rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT, and the Adaptix C2 framework. No oil or gas victim has been reported. The relevance is twofold: stolen HMI source gives an attacker a head start on finding flaws in products that end up in process plants, and O&G engineering teams and integrators increasingly keep PLC logic, HMI projects and SIS configuration in exactly this kind of self-hosted Git server.
tags: Threat Intelligence — PRC-linked campaign, SCADA/HMI source code theft

items.title: The NCSC says OT targeting is up across multiple sectors globally and has already caused real-world disruption — and that you should not assume your OT is unreachable
items.content_text: The UK National Cyber Security Centre published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, and that the activity has resulted in some limited real-world disruption. It names no victims, actors or techniques. The part worth reading in an oil and gas control room is the framing: organisations should not assume their OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. That describes the dispersed upstream and midstream estate almost exactly — wellpads, remote valve and meter stations, compressor sites and offshore telemetry commissioned by a contractor, connected over cellular or satellite, and rarely re-surveyed afterwards. The alert sets out eight actions covering internet exposure, credentials, boundary-device support, controller modes, logging and restoration.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks — energy incidents so far are landing on IT, and that is where the outage comes from
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — about 32 a day, a 23 percent rise on July’s 809 and above the previous monthly record of 988 in February 2025. Attacks on businesses reached 861 and on healthcare 69, while attacks on utilities doubled from five to ten. Qilin, with 157 claims, and The Gentlemen, with 107, together accounted for more than a quarter of the total. Treat the absolute numbers with caution: counts of this kind rest largely on leak-site claims and disclosure practice, and a claimed victim is not a confirmed one. The data does not break out oil and gas. The pattern it fits is nonetheless the one the sector already knows from Colonial Pipeline onward — encryption lands on business systems, and operations stop because scheduling, billing, custody-transfer accounting or terminal ticketing depends on them, not because anything touched a controller.

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect — and a planning horizon of three months running isolated
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released on 28 July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. The step that changes the engineering is keeping monitoring alive after the link is cut, because an isolation plan that also blinds the control room will not be executed under pressure. The addition worth arguing about is the planning horizon: Nozomi suggests operators assume they may need to sustain isolated operations for up to three months. For a pipeline or a refinery that pushes the question beyond network design into leak-detection models that pull data from enterprise systems, licence servers, time synchronisation, and how long a DCS can run without its business-network dependencies.

items.title: Nozomi chains 12 flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 to root on an OT edge device — patched, and not exploited
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client releases through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory with fixes in V4.0 HF0 and later. Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of edge services and lateral movement into the networks the device sits between. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth keeping apart: CISA updated the long-standing advisory ICSA-25-135-18 on 15 September to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes — an advisory update, not a new vulnerability — and this 18 September publication is the research behind it. The CVE identifiers in this set carry 2025 prefixes despite the 2026 disclosure, which is consistent with how the line was assigned but worth confirming against Siemens’ own advisory before you put them in a ticket. Our sector read: local processing engines and SINEMA remote access are used for edge processing and vendor connectivity at remote and unmanned sites, which is where root on an edge box buys the most.
tags: Research — OT edge device, vendor-patched vulnerability chain

items.title: A hard-coded key and MD5 password hashes inside AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor — read access to the project files is enough
items.content_text: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-253-01 on 10 September covering four vulnerabilities in the PIMBoards component of AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor, AVEVA’s real-time leak-detection and integrity product for liquid and gas pipelines. All versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1 are affected. CVE-2026-81821, a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVSS v3 8.4), lets anyone who can read PIMBoards project files decrypt the sensitive information inside them. CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing (CVSS v3 8.4), exposes password hashes to brute force and a potential route to administrator access. CVE-2026-81823, missing authorisation (5.3), allows unauthorised reads of PIMBoards data, and CVE-2026-81824, a cross-site scripting flaw (4.7), lets a malicious link run script in a user’s session. AVEVA found the first two itself; researcher Adham Khairy Ramadan reported the others. The fix is the 2025 SP1 P2 security update, and AVEVA notes that migrating legacy project files to the new cryptography is one-way. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most directly pipeline-specific advisory of the period: whoever can read or administer PIM can see, and potentially change, the leak-detection configuration and dashboards that controllers rely on for safety decisions.
tags: Critical Advisory — Pipeline leak detection and integrity monitoring

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Pipeline leak detection and integrity monitoring
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-253-01 and AVEVA security bulletin, reported by ISSSource and SecurityWeek

items.title: Schneider fixes a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety — and SCADAPack RTUs are in the same release
items.content_text: Schneider Electric’s September Patch Tuesday release on 8 September included SEVD-2026-251-04 for CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) scored CVSS v4.0 9.2. The weakness is exposed when a project built at a lower application level runs, and can affect confidentiality, integrity and availability. Affected are Modicon M580 at application levels below 4.00 and Modicon M580 Safety below 4.20; Blastwave’s analysis says Modicon MC80 is also affected. The same release fixed a medium-severity defect in SCADAPack x70 RTUs and a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300, and updated four existing advisories. Nothing in the release is reported as exploited. The sector relevance is our assessment rather than the vendor’s: M580 and M580 Safety controllers run process and safety functions in gas processing, terminals and refinery units, and SCADAPack RTUs are a common choice for wellsite automation and pipeline telemetry. An authentication weakness in a safety-rated controller is the kind of finding that belongs in the SIS change process, not the general patch queue.
tags: Critical Advisory — Process and safety controller authentication

items.title: A Sandworm-linked cluster and a Qilin ransomware operator got into Cisco firewall management consoles — the consoles that set your IT/OT boundary rules
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. It is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three post-compromise clusters. UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 and is not attributed to a named actor. UAT-11823, an APT whose tooling overlaps with the Russian group Sandworm, used CVE-2026-20079 together with CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a variant of Cyclops Blink — Talos does not say Sandworm itself was responsible. UAT-11988, assessed as a ransomware operator, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a static-credential flaw, and ultimately deployed Qilin. No OT impact and no oil and gas victim has been named. But FMC is where the firewall policy between corporate networks and plant, pipeline SCADA and terminal control networks is written, so root on FMC is the ability to quietly loosen that boundary.
tags: Critical Advisory — Exploited firewall management platform, CISA KEV

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited firewall management platform, CISA KEV

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited — and CISA says patching alone does not close it
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway are being exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance. CISA added both to KEV on 2 September with a 5 September federal deadline and flagged both for forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching does not end the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. Remote-access gateways like this are how automation vendors, integrators and on-call engineers reach DCS, SCADA and terminal systems out of hours, which makes the appliance a boundary device whether or not it is inventoried as one.
tags: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited remote-access gateway, KEV-listed

items.title: CISA’s 8 September KEV batch is led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your managed-service provider may use
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor fixes available. The one that matters most for oil and gas operations is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection weakness giving pre-authentication remote code execution on the remote monitoring and management server. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal deadline of 11 September has passed. RMM agents run with high privilege on the hosts they manage, and at smaller producers, midstream gathering operators and fuel distributors, IT is frequently outsourced to an MSP whose agents sit on the same Windows servers that host historians, SCADA clients or terminal automation. The batch also carries two exploited Windows privilege-escalation zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw.
tags: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited RMM platform, KEV-listed

items.title: CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including ScreenConnect — the remote-support tool that turns up on vendor-supplied OT PCs
items.content_text: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the KEV catalog on 12 September on evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload; and the RouterOS entry reflects the CERT Polska chain covered separately on this page. No oil and gas victim is named. The ScreenConnect entry is the one to read twice: remote-support tools are how OEM service desks and integrators reach compressor-control panels, analyser shelters, terminal automation PCs and engineering workstations, and they are often installed by the vendor rather than by the operator’s own security team.
tags: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited remote-support and build tooling

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited remote-support and build tooling
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026

items.title: “MikroTrick” is now confirmed exploited — two CVSS 9.2 SSH flaws hand over RouterOS admin on the routers at remote sites
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS chain known as “MikroTrick”, disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited, is being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CISA added the exploited flaws to KEV on 12 September. CERT Polska named no victims or sectors, only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks, so there is no confirmed oil and gas victim. It earns its place here because inexpensive, capable routers are a common contractor choice for cellular and fixed-wireless backhaul at wellpads, tank batteries, remote valve and meter stations — often the one device on site with a route to both the SCADA host and the internet.
tags: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers

items.title: Dutch NCSC warns exploitation of two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws is imminent — patches landed 9 September
items.content_text: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre issued a warning, reported on 12 September, that it expects near-term exploitation of two critical vulnerabilities in Check Point VPN products, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both carrying CVSS 9.8 in reporting. The pair can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can also affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. No public proof-of-concept had been reported and no exploitation confirmed at the time of the warning — the NCSC’s position is a forecast, not an observation. Firewall and VPN gateways of this class commonly sit at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres, where they often terminate the vendor and contractor tunnels into those networks.
tags: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent

items.title: September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships nine advisories and starts fixing the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw across its product lines
items.content_text: Siemens published nine new advisories and updated nine existing ones in the 8 September ICS patch round. The critical-severity findings are in the Reyrolle 7SR5 relay family, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT; Desigo CC, Teamcenter, the Mendix SAML module and Element Maps received high-severity fixes. Siemens also began shipping updates across affected products for the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” vulnerability, CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8, which can give a local attacker a root shell. In the same cycle Schneider Electric fixed the Modicon M580 authentication flaw covered separately above, and AVEVA published the Pipeline Integrity Monitor advisory also covered above, while noting a previously disclosed medium-severity deserialisation issue in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited. Most of Siemens’ items are grid, building or edge products rather than oil and gas specific, but Industrial Edge and embedded Linux devices appear in upstream and refinery digitalisation projects, and AVEVA Enterprise SCADA is widely used for pipeline control.
tags: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday round-up

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday round-up

items.title: Rockwell patches more than a dozen flaws in early September — RSLinx Classic, Logix controllers and the 1756-ENBT module among them
items.content_text: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, five of them Rockwell Automation, and SecurityWeek’s round-up on 2 September counted more than a dozen Rockwell vulnerabilities across products. ICSA-26-244-01 covers four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, -9622, -9624 and -9625 — each triggerable remotely with a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet and no authentication, fixed in 4.60. Other advisories reach the Logix platform, including ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380, the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool and FactoryTalk Activation Manager. SecurityWeek also reports a denial-of-service issue in the 1756-ENBT communications module, published by CISA as ICSA-26-246-05, and a high-severity remote code execution flaw in FactoryTalk Historian. One controller flaw, CVE-2026-9637, was initially described as exploited; that was corrected, and CISA confirmed no known exploitation. ControlLogix and CompactLogix chassis with 1756-ENBT modules are common in compressor stations, gas processing, loading racks and wellsite automation, where a controller or communications crash can trip or stall the process.
tags: Critical Advisory — Vendor patches, Logix controllers and communications

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patches, Logix controllers and communications

items.title: A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco ISE is being exploited — the policy engine that decides who gets onto your network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Cisco Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco states that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation, and all versions are affected until patched: 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4 carry the fix. There are no workarounds; Cisco points to infrastructure ACLs restricting management traffic as the only mitigation. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September. No actor has been named, no indicators beyond checking access logs for unfamiliar usernames have been published, and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed. The sector relevance is our assessment: ISE is the NAC and 802.1X policy engine that, in many operators, decides which devices and which vendor sessions are allowed onto the industrial DMZ and the plant network. Administrative control of it is administrative control of your segmentation policy.
tags: Critical Advisory — Exploited network access control platform, CISA KEV

items.title: A crafted email is enough: Cisco Secure Email Gateway SQL injection exploited as a zero-day, root without user interaction
items.content_text: Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX, first published 14 September, covers CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 SQL-injection flaw in AsyncOS email parsing on Cisco Secure Email Gateway. An unauthenticated attacker who sends a specially crafted email can run arbitrary SQL and then commands as root, with no user interaction and regardless of appliance configuration; physical and virtual appliances are both affected. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026. Fixed builds are available, with 16.5.0-780 the preferred target and separate fixed builds for the 16.0 and 15.5 trains — outlets have printed inconsistent build strings, so take yours from the Cisco advisory. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 14 September with a federal deadline of 17 September, now passed. Shadowserver counted more than 400 exposed appliances. No attribution has been published and no industrial targeting has been reported. This is an IT mail gateway, not an OT device, and we list it for one reason: it is an unauthenticated, no-click path to root inside the enterprise that hosts your engineering workstations, historians and remote-access brokers.

items.title: mySCADA myPRO Manager hands privileged management functions to anyone who can reach it — CVSS 9.8, fixed in 2.2
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-03, published 15 September, covers two flaws in mySCADA myPRO Manager. CVE-2026-73807, CVSS v3 9.8, is a missing-authorisation flaw in the command API: an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the interface gets privileged management functions. CVE-2026-82567, CVSS 6.3 and adjacent-network only, allows unauthenticated sending of arbitrary SMS messages through a connected GSM modem. Versions up to and including 2.1 are affected; 2.2 is the fix. CISA lists Energy among the affected sectors, alongside Water and Wastewater, Critical Manufacturing, Food and Agriculture and Transportation, and states that no public exploitation targeting these flaws has been reported to it. The sector read is ours: myPRO is an inexpensive HMI and SCADA package that turns up at small and unmanned sites — gathering systems, small gas plants, tank farms and contractor-supplied skids — typically behind a cellular router with SMS alerting attached. Those are exactly the deployments least likely to appear in a corporate asset register.

items.title: CISA republishes the SCADAPack x70 credential flaw — the RTU family at wellheads, metering runs and compressor stations
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-04, published 15 September, republishes Schneider Electric’s 8 September notice SEVD-2026-251-03 and gives the flaw an identifier: CVE-2026-81861, CVSS v3 6.5 (v4 5.9), insufficiently protected credentials in the Secure Lock function. The consequence is unauthorised access to RTU configuration. The advisory lists SCADAPack 47x, 47xi, 47xd, 470R and 57x, with the product tree also naming SCADAPack 3xx and 32; CISA records the affected sectors as Critical Manufacturing and Energy. No code fix is listed in CISA’s machine-readable advisory — the remedies are configuration: enable role-based access control as set out in Schneider’s SCADAPack security guidelines, segment the RTU networks, and use the RTU Firewall Service to restrict which services are reachable. No exploitation has been reported. This is the CVE detail behind the SCADAPack line in Schneider’s September release, and it matters here more than the score suggests: these are the remote units that report and control at unmanned sites, often over cellular or licensed radio, where “who can read the configuration” is not a theoretical question.

items.title: About 20 flaws in one shared IO-Link master firmware base hit three vendors at once — unauthenticated root at the field layer
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published three advisories on 16 September that carry the same CVE range, CVE-2026-27546 through CVE-2026-27565, across three different brands: VDE-2026-014 for Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-* and ICE3-* models, VDE-2026-027 for Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8, and VDE-2026-028 for Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 units. One shared CVE set across three vendors points to a common OEM firmware base. The worst two are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an OS command injection at CVSS 9.8 reachable over the network without authentication or user interaction; below them sit command-injection and local-file-inclusion flaws at 8.8, an authorisation bypass at 8.1, path traversal at 7.5 and information disclosure at 6.5. The outcome is unauthenticated root code execution on the device and theft of stored password hashes and SSH private keys. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and the advisories name 1.7.8 as fixed — confirm the exact build with your vendor. No exploitation has been reported. IO-Link masters aggregate sensors and actuators onto EtherNet/IP and PROFINET segments; in oil and gas they usually arrive inside packaged equipment — metering and analyser cabinets, custody-transfer skids, vendor process packages — rather than in the main DCS I/O count, which is why they are easy to miss.

items.title: Six CISA ICS advisories on 17 September — Hitachi Energy FACTS, two Schneider products, Mitsubishi GX Works3, ABB Edgenius and an ELD
items.content_text: CISA released six ICS advisories on Thursday 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -06: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), and ABB Ability Edgenius. Detail is verified for the first two only. GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings carry CVE-2026-15688, an authentication algorithm flaw scored CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7, affecting all versions and enabling local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs. The Bransys electronic logging device has three hardcoded or cleartext credential flaws — CVE-2026-86520 (7.5), CVE-2026-86689 (5.9) and CVE-2026-77960 (5.3) — fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. For the other four advisories, CISA’s machine-readable files had not reached the public mirror at the time of writing, so we are deliberately not printing severity scores or sector lists for them; read the advisory pages before you triage. CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07, the Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN advisory, on 17 September, adding eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch. The two worth an oil and gas look are Modicon M340, a controller family common in utilities and balance-of-plant duties, and Edgenius, an industrial edge platform — judge both against your own estate rather than the sector labels.

items.title: The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — relevant to every waterfront oil and LNG terminal it regulates
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has established the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG-MCP) under its Director of Inspections and Compliance, as the central authority for cybersecurity policy across the Marine Transportation System. Its remit is to develop domestic policy, contribute to international standards, direct a unified compliance and enforcement strategy, and serve as the main point of contact for industry. The move follows Government Accountability Office findings on gaps in Coast Guard cyber oversight, including weak incident tracking and missing personnel competency standards. Nothing in the maritime cyber rule changes today. The relevance to oil and gas is that the Coast Guard is the security regulator for waterfront facilities handling crude, refined products and LNG, and it was Coast Guard cyber teams, with the FBI, that boarded the US-bound tankers in the top story. Consolidating policy and compliance under one office usually means the same questions, asked the same way, at more facilities.

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance — the standard your shippers, customers and regulators will hold you to
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks providers to hold a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, send plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, give affected users root-cause and technical detail they can act on, and align messaging with legal and regulatory duties. Pipeline and terminal operators are service providers in exactly this sense. The 2021 Colonial Pipeline shutdown showed how quickly an unexplained halt becomes a fuel-supply and public-confidence problem when shippers, retailers and the public are left to fill the gap themselves.

items.title: 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the first hours of a pipeline incident are when they collide
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours when containment matters most. Oil and gas operators will recognise the shape. A single cyber event can touch TSA’s pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for marine terminals, SEC disclosure for listed companies, state regulators, cyber insurers and contractual notice to shippers and customers. The analysis lands as the CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn, which is when harmonisation either happens or does not.

items.title: CISA’s cyber decoys guide: tripwires and honeytokens as detection you can add without touching production
items.content_text: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence or support intelligence collection, and it structures deployment in three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions decoys alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for either segmentation or monitoring. The reason it is worth an oil and gas reader’s time is the constraint it fits: most detection improvements in OT require touching a production system, and decoys mostly do not. A fake engineering workstation credential that no legitimate process uses, a planted project file, a dormant account named to look like a vendor login — each of these produces a signal with a very low false-positive rate and no change to the control system itself. That makes it one of the few detection moves that can be made between turnarounds rather than during one.

items.title: CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — if your patch triage consumes it, change the input now
items.content_text: CISA is discontinuing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September 2026, reported on 17 September. The agency is pointing users instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, its alerts and its advisories, and frames the change as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in BOD 26-04 of June 2026. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected, and the KEV catalog continues unchanged. The practical point for operators is narrow but real: the weekly bulletin is a bulk feed that several vulnerability-management workflows and vendor summaries quietly depend on, and a feed that simply stops publishing tends to fail silently rather than loudly. If your process has a step that begins “each week, review the CISA vulnerability summary”, that step needs a new source before the end of the month.
